summaries.gardner: TJX is the top dog in off-price retail with well-known banners, but it is a mature, mid-single-digit-growth retailer rather than a leader of an emerging industry. Its stock has not had strong recent momentum (about +1.5% over 52 weeks) and it lacks the visionary-founder, new-industry traits Rule Breaker investing looks for.
summaries.buffett: TJX fits many Buffett tenets: a simple, understandable business, consistent profits for decades, high returns on equity (about 62% trailing), little financial debt ($2.9 billion against $6.0 billion cash) and a durable scale-based buying advantage. The main gap is price: at about 27 times trailing earnings it offers little margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Munger would value the simple, durable model, the frugal merchant culture and the scale advantages in buying that have compounded since 1977. Inverting, the business has few ways to fail, but at roughly 27 times earnings for 6-7% revenue growth it is a great business at a full price.
summaries.lynch: TJX is a classic Lynch stalwart: a store everyone knows, steady growth (sales up from $48.6 billion in FY2022 to $60.4 billion in FY2026), a falling share count and room to add stores toward a 7,500-store target. Its P/E of about 27 is well above its roughly 11% EPS growth, so on Lynch's PEG test it looks expensive.
summaries.fisher: TJX shows Fisher-like strengths in sales ability, an outstanding merchant organisation, long-term thinking and rising profit margins (gross margin from 28.5% in FY2022 to 31.0% in FY2026). It does not do research and development in the usual sense, so Fisher's product-innovation points fit only partly.
summaries.graham: TJX meets several defensive-investor criteria: it is large, profitable every year for over a decade, has paid dividends for decades and grew EPS far more than one third in ten years. It fails Graham's valuation tests badly, at about 27 times earnings and about 15 times book value.
summaries.thiel: TJX is not a Zero to One company: it has no proprietary technology that is ten times better and operates in a competitive market alongside Ross and Burlington. Its strengths are distribution and scale in buying, which make it durable but not a monopoly built on a secret.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner focuses on large secular platform shifts and growth at a reasonable price; TJX is a high-quality, efficiently run retailer but is not tied to AI or another major platform shift. With forward P/E near 27 and revenue growth around 6%, it does not match his growth-adjusted valuation lens.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller looks for earnings acceleration and catalysts; TJX's EPS growth did accelerate (diluted EPS up 26% in the first half of FY27, helped by one-time tariff refunds) and guidance was raised, but Marmaxx comp sales slowed to 1% and the share price has lagged. It is a defensive, low-beta (0.56) stock rather than a macro-driven high-conviction bet.
summaries.smith: TJX largely fits Terry Smith's 'good company' test: high returns on capital (ROIC about 30%), steady growth, strong cash generation ($4.9 billion of free cash flow in FY2026) and low cyclicality. The question for Smith would be valuation, with a free-cash-flow yield of only about 3%.
summaries.greenblatt: TJX scores very well on return on capital but poorly on earnings yield: trailing operating income of about $7.9 billion is roughly 5% of an enterprise value near $159 billion. It would likely rank mid-pack, not top, on the Magic Formula.
summaries.akre: TJX meets two legs of Akre's stool well: an extraordinary business with high returns on capital and talented, shareholder-minded management. The third leg, reinvestment, is moderate: it reinvests in new stores and countries but returns most cash through buybacks and a dividend raised 13% in 2026.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai seeks simple businesses bought at deep discounts with low downside; TJX is simple and has low risk of permanent loss, but it is not distressed or cheap. The Dhandho 'heads I win, tails I don't lose much' setup is missing at 27 times earnings.
summaries.wood: TJX has no exposure to ARK's innovation platforms such as AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or genomic sequencing. It is a store-based value retailer and does not fit Cathie Wood's disruptive-innovation framework.
summaries.ackman: TJX fits much of Ackman's checklist: a simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generating business with high barriers from scale, low debt and strong management. It lacks a clear catalyst or valuation discount, so it would appeal more as a quality compounder than an activist opportunity.
summaries.sleep: TJX resembles Nick Sleep's 'scale economics shared' model in part: its buying scale lets it keep prices 20-60% below full-price rivals, which keeps shoppers returning. Its revenue grows mid-single digits, so it is a steady rather than fast-compounding example.
summaries.valentine: Don Valentine's venture lens looks for huge new markets and technology shifts; TJX is a mature retailer in established apparel and home markets. It solves a real but ordinary problem (paying less for brand-name goods), so it is not a Sequoia-style opportunity.
summaries.nash: TJX passes Nash's quality screens on cash versus debt, institutional ownership, low short interest and beating expectations, but fails key growth and margin tests: revenue grows about 7% and operating margin is about 12-13%, below his 20% instant-kill line. Valuation is also stretched, with a PEG above 2 and a simple DCF far below the share price.

momentum.evidence: The share price was $147.33 on October 16, 2026, only about +1.5% over 52 weeks and below $156.75 at the end of April 2026, after falling to about $134 in August on slower Marmaxx sales.

g4.evidence: CEO Ernie Herrman (CEO since 2016, at TJX since 1989) leads a long-tenured merchant team, and about 94% of shares are held by institutions.

g6.evidence: Some analysts flag a full valuation (P/E about 27, PEG about 2.7, Wells Fargo Hold with $140 target), but most of 22 analysts rate it a Buy.

simple.evidence: TJX buys brand-name excess merchandise cheaply and sells it in 5,285 stores at big discounts; the model is easy to understand.

b2.evidence: TJX was profitable through the pandemic (net income of $90 million in FY2021) and sales grew every year from FY2022 to FY2026, reaching $60.4 billion.

integrity.evidence: TJX gives detailed guidance and separates one-time gains (the FY2026 interchange settlement and FY2027 IEEPA tariff refunds) from adjusted results, returns cash steadily, and uses PwC as auditor.

b6.evidence: TJX has grown mainly by opening its own stores and small joint ventures rather than large acquisitions, sticking to its off-price model.

roic.evidence: Return on equity is about 62% and ROIC about 30% with only $2.9 billion of debt against $6.0 billion cash; lease obligations of about $11.4 billion are its main fixed commitment.

fcf.evidence: FY2026 operating cash flow of $6,874 million less $1,957 million capex gives $4,917 million of free cash flow, about 90% of $5,494 million net income.

b10.evidence: Retained earnings funded store growth and buybacks that cut diluted shares from 1,216 million in FY2022 to 1,128 million in FY2026, while market value rose to about $162 billion.

safety.evidence: At $147.33 the stock trades at about 27 times trailing EPS of $5.40, and a conservative DCF gives about $64 per share, so there is no margin of safety.

fairprice.evidence: A forward P/E of about 27 for roughly 6% revenue and 11% EPS growth is a full price, though partly justified by TJX's quality and consistency.

mu5.evidence: With net cash, a value proposition that tends to do well in downturns and a diversified store base across nine countries, there are few obvious ways for the business to fail.

reinvest.evidence: TJX can keep reinvesting in new stores (store growth stepping up to 4% from FY28 toward 7,500 stores) at high returns, but that absorbs only part of its cash; most is returned to shareholders.

ly2.evidence: It is a stalwart with a simple story: keep adding stores and grow comp sales 2-4% while slowly expanding margins.

ly3.evidence: The P/E of about 27 is well above expected EPS growth of about 11% (consensus FY2027 EPS $5.25).

runway.evidence: Management targets 7,500 stores versus 5,285 in August 2026 and new markets such as Spain, giving years of mid-single-digit growth but not explosive growth.

ly7.evidence: The company is cutting its share count (8.9 million shares repurchased for $1.4 billion in the first half of FY27), but no notable insider open-market buying was found and insiders own about 0.12%.

ly8.evidence: TJX is a $162 billion company followed by 22 analysts and about 94% owned by institutions, though its business is 'boring' discount retail.

fi2.evidence: TJX keeps adding new formats and banners (Homesense, Sierra) and countries, but it has no product pipeline in the usual sense.

fi3.evidence: TJX does not report research and development spending; its investments go into stores, distribution and systems.

fi4.evidence: Its buying and selling machine turns inventory quickly and grew consolidated comp sales 5% in FY2026 with little advertising.

longterm.evidence: Management consistently invests in store growth, distribution centres and talent for the long term and frames goals around a 7,500-store long-term target.

gr1.evidence: TJX had $60.4 billion of FY2026 sales and a market value of about $162 billion.

ni10.evidence: TJX reported a profit in each of the last ten fiscal years, including $90 million in pandemic-hit FY2021 and $5,494 million in FY2026.

gr4.evidence: TJX has paid dividends for decades; in 2026 the CEO called the 13% raise 'our 29th dividend increase over the last 30 years'.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $2.70 in FY2022 to $4.87 in FY2026 alone, far more than one third growth, and ten-year growth is larger still.

gr6.evidence: The share price is about 27 times trailing EPS, well above Graham's limit of about 15.

gr7.evidence: P/E of about 27 times price-to-book of about 15 gives roughly 415, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: TJX has no proprietary technology ten times better than rivals; its edge is buying scale and know-how.

timing.evidence: Value-seeking shoppers and excess branded inventory from tariff-driven disruption favour off-price retailers now, but there is no new technology or market timing story.

th3.evidence: T.J. Maxx started in 1977 as a leader in a small off-price niche and expanded into home goods and nine countries, though that niche is now large and mature.

team.evidence: TJX's management, led by career merchant Ernie Herrman, is widely respected for consistent execution and has delivered results above plan in recent quarters.

th5.evidence: Its 5,285 stores and six e-commerce sites give it a massive physical distribution network to reach shoppers.

durable.evidence: Off-price has gained share for decades and TJX's buying scale with about 21,000 vendors should remain relevant in 10-20 years, though online value rivals are a risk.

th7.evidence: Off-price retail is well understood and contested by Ross, Burlington and Nordstrom Rack.

trend.evidence: TJX is not a beneficiary of AI, cloud or another platform shift; it rides the slower trend of shoppers trading down to value.

dr1.evidence: First-half FY27 diluted EPS rose 26% to $2.55 and full-year guidance was raised to $5.31-5.36, but part of that came from one-time tariff refunds and Marmaxx comps slowed to 1%.

dr2.evidence: Store growth stepping up to 4% from FY28 and international expansion could help, but it is unclear whether results will beat what the market already expects.

dr4.evidence: Value retailers tend to gain share when consumers are squeezed, but tariffs and wage costs are headwinds; with net cash, interest rates matter little.

dr6.evidence: Further IEEPA tariff refunds (expected in Q3 FY27), new countries such as Spain, and faster store openings are possible drivers, though the company calls refund amounts uncertain.

dr7.evidence: A steady, fully valued mid-single-digit grower is unlikely to justify a large, concentrated macro-style position.

gm.evidence: Gross margin (after buying and occupancy costs) is about 31.0%, typical of discount retail and not a sign of strong pricing power.

fcfyield.evidence: FY2026 free cash flow of $4.9 billion is about 3.0% of a $162 billion market value, modest but reasonable for a high-quality, low-risk retailer.

gb2.evidence: Trailing operating income of about $7.9 billion is only about 5% of enterprise value of about $159 billion.

pa2.evidence: TJX is not in a setback; aside from Marmaxx's 1% Q2 comp, it is posting record results.

pa4.evidence: Net cash, a consistently profitable model and diversified banners make permanent loss of capital unlikely, though valuation risk exists.

wo1.evidence: TJX is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing.

wo2.evidence: Its costs are mainly merchandise, wages and occupancy, which do not fall quickly with volume.

wo3.evidence: TJX does not combine several innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: Its addressable apparel and home markets grow slowly and cannot become many times larger in five years.

ac3.evidence: With net cash it is insulated from interest rates, but tariffs, freight and wage costs affect it directly.

ns1.evidence: TJX uses its buying scale to keep prices 20-60% below full-price retailers' regular prices, reinforcing its value lead over smaller rivals.

ns4.evidence: It should be larger with more stores and countries in 10-20 years, but whether its competitive position is clearly stronger depends on online value competition.

va2.evidence: It helps families stretch budgets on clothing and home goods, a real but not a large, painful problem.

tn1.evidence: TJX is a store-based retailer, not a company built for a secular trend such as AI, energy or robotics.

tn2.evidence: The market sees TJX as a high-quality off-price retailer, which is what it is; there is no hidden transformation.

tn3.evidence: It is a large US company, not a small cap, Chinese company, commodity producer or airline, but retail sales are somewhat seasonal with a holiday-heavy fourth quarter.

tn4.evidence: It passes all three: revenue grew every year from FY2022 to FY2026, net income was $5,494 million in FY2026, and cash of $6,004 million exceeds debt of $2,871 million.

tn5.evidence: Cash exceeded debt on every recent balance sheet ($6.2 billion vs $2.9 billion at FY2026 end, $5.6 billion and $6.0 billion in Q1 and Q2 FY27) and FY2026 and first-half FY27 free cash flow were positive, but each quarter's free cash flow was not separately checked.

tn6.evidence: Revenue grew 7.1% in FY2026 and 7.2% in the first half of FY27, below 10%.

tn7.evidence: Revenue growth of about 7% plus FY2026 free-cash-flow margin of about 8.1% gives about 15, well below 40.

tn8.evidence: In FY2026 net sales grew 7.1% while cost of sales plus SG&A grew about 6.3% ($50,058 million to $53,194 million).

tn9.evidence: It fails the instant-kill test on operating margin, which is about 12-13%, below 20%; it passes on size, net cash, short interest (about 1.7%) and age.

tn10.evidence: No major regulatory or legal threat is known; its notable recent litigation was as a plaintiff, winning a credit card interchange fee settlement.

tn11.evidence: TJX provides brand-name apparel and home goods at 20-60% below full-price retailers that help budget-minded shoppers get quality for less, and earns a retail markup on merchandise bought cheaply from about 21,000 vendors.

tn13.evidence: Total about 80: cash vs debt 10, revenue growth 0, operating margin 5, short interest 10, institutional ownership 10, revenue faster than expenses 10, 5-year return vs S&P 10 (price roughly $65 in October 2021 to $147, estimated well ahead of the index), moat 5, CEO 5, recession-proof pricing power 5, secular trend 0, culture and mission 5, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Revenue grew every year from FY2022 to FY2026 and free cash flow stayed positive, but operating margin dipped in FY2023 (about 9.7% vs 9.8%) and free cash flow fell from $4,335 million in FY2024 to $4,198 million in FY2025.

tn15.evidence: Interest coverage is very high (net interest income), the current ratio is 1.15 and liabilities are about 2.5 times equity, but assets excluding goodwill ($37.0 billion) are only about 1.4 times liabilities ($26.5 billion) because of lease liabilities.

tn18.evidence: Herrman has about 10 years as CEO and a strong execution record, but he is not a founder and no open-market share purchases by him were found.

tn20.evidence: TJX reported results 'well above plan' in Q4 FY26, Q1 FY27 (EPS $1.19 vs guidance of $0.97-0.99) and Q2 FY27 ($1.36 diluted EPS), and raised guidance.

tn21.evidence: No major red flags: a single CEO, no acquisition spree, PwC as long-standing auditor and rising margins, but year-end inventory rose 13.6% ($6,421 million to $7,297 million) against 7.1% sales growth in FY2026, a point to watch.

tn22.evidence: TJX has $60 billion of revenue, strong profits and buys back shares rather than issuing them.

tn24.evidence: At a free-cash-flow yield of about 3%, the price implies growth of free cash flow faster than the roughly 6-7% revenue growth TJX is delivering.

tn25.evidence: Using 3-year averages (revenue growth about 6.5%, FCF margin about 7.9%), 4% terminal growth and a 12% discount rate, value is about $64 per share, well below $147.33.

tn26.evidence: Forward P/E is about 27 against consensus EPS growth of about 11% for FY2027, a PEG of roughly 2.5-2.7, well above 1.
